nodes.name: Willmore surface
nodes.statement:
A Willmore surface is, by definition, a critical point of the
  Willmore functional 
  $$
    \mathcal{W}(\Sigma) = \int_\Sigma H^2 \,d\mu
  $$
  where $H=\frac{1}{2}(k_1+k_2)$ is the mean curvature, $k_1,k_2$ are the principal curvatures and where  
  $d\mu$ denotes the associated volume form of the surface.
nodes.origin_citation: standard (uncited)
nodes.statement_short: A Willmore surface is a critical point of the Willmore functional, the integral of squared mean curvature.

nodes.name: elasticae (elastic curves in the hyperbolic plane)
nodes.statement:
It it known \cite{LanSing_Curves_in_the}
  that Willmore surfaces of revolution are generated by elastic curves in the hyperbolic
  plane $\mathbb{H}$ (called elasticae), which, by definition, are critical for the total squared curvature
  functional.
nodes.origin_citation: Langer & Singer 1984 (curves in the hyperbolic plane)
differentia: critical for the total squared curvature functional
nodes.statement_short: Willmore surfaces of revolution are generated by elasticae: curves in H critical for total squared curvature.

nodes.name: Langer-Singer classification of closed elasticae in H
nodes.statement: Let $\gamma$ be a regular closed curve in $\mathbb{H}$ which is critical for the elastic energy functional. Then either $\gamma$ is the $m$-fold cover of the ball for some $m$, or $\gamma$ is a member of the family of solutions $\gamma_{m,n}$ having the following description: if $m>1$ and $n$ are integers satisfying $1<\frac{2m}{n}<\sqrt{2}$ there is (up to congruence) a unique curve $\gamma_{m,n}$, which closes up in $n$ periods of its curvature $\kappa=\kappa_0 \mathrm{cn}^2(rs,p)$ while making $m$ orbits about the fixed point of the associated rotation field $J$. Further, $\gamma_{m,n}$ oscillates between a pair of invariant circles of $J$ with the $n$ maxima of $\kappa$ equally spaced around the outer circle and the $n$ minima of $\kappa$ equally spaced around the inner circle. Also, $\gamma_{m,n}$ has $n(m-1)$ points of selfintersections.
nodes.origin_citation: Langer & Singer 1984 (curves in the hyperbolic plane)
assumptions: $\gamma$ be a regular closed curve in $\mathbb{H}$ which is critical for the elastic energy functional
conclusions: either $\gamma$ is the $m$-fold cover of the ball for some $m$, or $\gamma$ is a member of the family of solutions $\gamma_{m,n}$
Also, $\gamma_{m,n}$ has $n(m-1)$ points of selfintersections.
nodes.statement_short: Closed elasticae in H are multiple covers of a circle or curves gamma_{m,n} with 1<2m/n<sqrt2, oscillating between circles with n(m-1) selfintersections.
nodes.label: thm:LanSin

nodes.name: Typo in the Langer-Singer curvature formula
nodes.statement:
Notice that $\kappa=\kappa_0 \mathrm{cn}^2(rs,p)$ is a typo in \cite{LanSing_Curves_in_the} since the curvature
  function is basically a $\mathrm{dn}$-function (cf. \eqref{eq:def_kappa_orbitlike}), as we will see later.

nodes.name: orbitlike elastica
nodes.statement:
Following \cite{LanSing_Curves_in_the} (not necessarily closed) elastic curves generated by such
  curvature functions will be called orbitlike.
nodes.origin_citation: Langer & Singer 1984 (curves in the hyperbolic plane)

nodes.name: surface of revolution generated by a curve
nodes.statement_short: Sigma_gamma is the surface of revolution generated by the curve gamma about the x1-axis.

nodes.name: Surface of revolution Sigma_gamma
nodes.statement: \Sigma_\gamma = \Big\{ (\gamma_1(s),\gamma_2(s)\cos(t),\gamma_2(s)\sin(t)) : s\in I, t\in [0,2\pi) \Big\}
nodes.label: eq:Sigma_gamma

nodes.name: Dirichlet problem for Willmore surfaces of revolution
nodes.statement:
The problem
  then is to find a Willmore surface with preassigned initial or end positions and angles, i.e. for given
  $(A_1,A_2),(B_1,B_2)$ in the hyperbolic plane and $\phi_A,\phi_B\in\mathbb{R}$ one has to find an elastic curve
  $\gamma$ with (unknown) hyperbolic length $L$ such that the following holds:
  \begin{equation} \mathcal{W}'(\Sigma_\gamma)=0,\quad  \gamma(0)=(A_1,A_2),\quad \gamma(L)=(B_1,B_2),\quad
    e^{i\phi(0)}=e^{i\phi_A},\quad e^{i\phi(L)}=e^{i\phi_B}. 
  \end{equation}
  Here, we formally write $\mathcal{W}'(\Sigma_\gamma)=0$ in place of the Willmore equation and the
  angle function $\phi$ is given by $\gamma'=|\gamma'|e^{i\phi}$.
nodes.statement_short: Find an elastica with prescribed endpoints and endpoint angles generating a Willmore surface of revolution.

nodes.name: Dirichlet boundary value problem
nodes.statement: \mathcal{W}'(\Sigma_\gamma)=0,\quad \gamma(0)=(A_1,A_2),\quad \gamma(L)=(B_1,B_2),\quad e^{i\phi(0)}=e^{i\phi_A},\quad e^{i\phi(L)}=e^{i\phi_B}.
nodes.label: eq:DirichletBVP

nodes.name: Existence of graphical solutions for symmetric Dirichlet data
nodes.statement:
One example for a result in the graphical setting
  can be found in the papers \cite{DalAcDecGru_Classical_solutions,DalAcFroGruSch_Symmetric}: For
  $A_1=-B_1,A_2=B_2$ and $\phi_A=-\phi_B \in [0,\pi/2)$ the Dirichlet problem has a graphical solution which,
  by Theorem~1.1 in \cite{Eich_nonuniqueness}, may in general fail to be unique.
nodes.origin_citation: Dall'Acqua, Deckelnick, Grunau; Dall'Acqua, Froehlich, Grunau, Schieweck
conclusions: the Dirichlet problem has a graphical solution

nodes.name: Symmetry of orbitlike solutions for symmetric Dirichlet data
nodes.statement: Assume $A_1=-B_1\neq 0, A_2=B_2>0,\phi_A+\phi_B\in 2\pi\mathbb{Z}$ such that $$ \pm\big(\frac{A_2}{A_1}\sin(\phi_A) + \cos(\phi_A)\big) \notin (0,2). $$ Then all positively $(\pm=+)$ respectively negatively $(\pm=-)$ oriented orbitlike solutions of~\eqref{eq:DirichletBVP} are symmetric.
also_stated_at: Assume $A_1=-B_1\neq 0, A_2=B_2>0,\phi_A+\phi_B\in 2\pi\mathbb{Z}$ such that $$ \pm\big(\frac{A_2}{A_1}\sin(\phi_A) + \cos(\phi_A)\big) \notin (0,2). $$ Then all positively $(\pm=+)$ respectively negatively $(\pm=-)$ oriented orbitlike solutions of~\eqref{eq:DirichletBVP} are symmetric.
conclusions: all positively $(\pm=+)$ respectively negatively $(\pm=-)$ oriented orbitlike solutions of~\eqref{eq:DirichletBVP} are symmetric.
nodes.statement_short: Under symmetric boundary data with A1=-B1 nonzero and an angle condition, all orbitlike solutions of a given orientation are symmetric.
nodes.label: thm:Symmetry

nodes.name: symmetric solution
nodes.statement:
Here, a solution of \eqref{eq:DirichletBVP} is called symmetric if we have
  $$
    \gamma_1(L/2+s)=-\gamma_1(L/2-s),\quad \gamma_2(L/2+s)=\gamma_1(L/2-s)
    \qquad\text{for all }s\in [0,L/2]
  $$ 
  and it is called nonsymmetric otherwise.

nodes.name: positive / negative orientation
nodes.statement:
Positive / negative orientation means that the
  hyperbolic curvature of the elastica is assumed to be positive / negative at some point (and hence
  everywhere since the $\mathrm{dn}$-function is zero-free).

nodes.name: Symmetry for Koeller-Eichmann boundary data
nodes.statement:
In particular, negatively oriented elasticae are
  symmetric when $A_1=-B_1=-1,A_2=B_2=\alpha>0,\phi_A=\phi_B=0$, which corresponds to the boundary data studied by
  Koeller and Eichmann in Theorem~1.1~\cite{Eich_symmetry}.
conclusions: negatively oriented elasticae are symmetric

nodes.name: Symmetry breaking for the Dirichlet problem
nodes.statement: There are boundary data $A_1=-B_1,A_2=B_2>0,\phi_A=-\phi_B$ such that \eqref{eq:DirichletBVP} has uncountably many nonsymmetric solutions.
conclusions: There are boundary data $A_1=-B_1,A_2=B_2>0,\phi_A=-\phi_B$ such that \eqref{eq:DirichletBVP} has uncountably many nonsymmetric solutions.
nodes.label: thm:Symmetry_breaking

nodes.name: hyperbolic plane
nodes.statement:
Willmore surfaces of revolution are known to be generated by elastic curves in the hyperbolic plane
  $\mathbb{H}=\{(x_1,x_2)\in\mathbb{R}^2: x_2>0\}$, see for instance p.532 in \cite{LanSing_Curves_in_the}.
nodes.origin_citation: standard (uncited)

nodes.name: hyperbolic metric and distance
nodes.statement:
The
  metric is given by $\frac{dx_1^2+dx_2^2}{x_2^2}$ 
  and the distance between 
  two points $(x_1,x_2),(y_1,y_2)\in \mathbb{H}$ is 
  \begin{equation} d_{\mathbb{H}}((x_1,x_2),(y_1,y_2)) 
      =  \mathrm{Arcosh}\Big(1+\frac{(x_1-y_1)^2+(x_2-y_2)^2}{2x_2y_2}\Big). 
      
	
  \end{equation}
nodes.origin_citation: standard (uncited)

nodes.name: Hyperbolic distance formula
nodes.origin_citation: standard (uncited)
nodes.label: eq:metric

nodes.name: hyperbolic arclength parametrization
nodes.statement:
Regular curves $\gamma$ in $\mathbb{H}$ are therefore parametrized by hyperbolic arclength if
  $(\gamma_1')^2+(\gamma_2')^2\equiv \gamma_2^2$ and in fact all curves studied in this paper will be written
  down in this parametrization.
nodes.origin_citation: standard (uncited)

nodes.name: angle function and hyperbolic curvature
nodes.statement:
Introducing the angle  function $\phi$ via 
  $\gamma_1' = \gamma_2 \cos(\phi),\gamma_2' = \gamma_2 \sin(\phi)$ (such that $\gamma'=|\gamma'|e^{i\phi}$) 
  one finds that the hyperbolic (or geodesic) curvature function is given by
    \begin{equation} \kappa
      := - \frac{\gamma_2^2}{\gamma_2'} \Big(\frac{\gamma_1'}{\gamma_2^2}\Big)' 
      = \phi'+\cos(\phi).
    \end{equation}
nodes.origin_citation: standard (uncited)
nodes.statement_short: The angle function phi with gamma' = |gamma'| e^{i phi}, and the hyperbolic curvature kappa = phi' + cos(phi).

nodes.name: Hyperbolic curvature formula
nodes.statement: \kappa := - \frac{\gamma_2^2}{\gamma_2'} \Big(\frac{\gamma_1'}{\gamma_2^2}\Big)' = \phi'+\cos(\phi).
nodes.origin_citation: standard (uncited)
nodes.label: eq:hyperbolic_curvature

nodes.name: ODE system recovering a curve from its curvature
nodes.statement: \gamma_1' = \gamma_2 \cos(\phi),\quad \gamma_2' = \gamma_2 \sin(\phi),\quad \phi' + \cos(\phi) = \kappa.
nodes.label: eq:ODE_solution

nodes.name: Invariance under hyperbolic isometries
nodes.statement:
This ODE system is invariant under M\"obius transformations and in particular under the continuous
    isometries of the hyperbolic plane where only the initial data $\gamma_1(0),\gamma_2(0),\phi(0)$ changes.
    Identifying $\mathbb{H}$ with $\{x+iy:y>0\}$ and writing $\gamma=\gamma_1+i\gamma_2$ these isometries take the
    following form:
    \begin{itemize}
      \item[(i)] horizontal translation: $\gamma\mapsto \gamma+a$ for $a\in\mathbb{R}$,
      \item[(ii)] dilation: $\gamma \mapsto b\gamma$ for $b>0$,
      \item[(iii)] hyperbolic rotation: $\gamma\mapsto 
      \tfrac{\cos(\theta/2)\gamma+\sin(\theta/2)}{-\sin(\theta/2)\gamma+\cos(\theta/2)}
      
      $ for $\theta\in\mathbb{R}$.
    \end{itemize}
    The missing isometries are discrete and come from reflections, i.e. horizontal reflection and inversion
    with respect to the unit sphere. Notice that both cause a sign change in the curvature function.
nodes.origin_citation: standard (uncited)
nodes.statement_short: The curve ODE is invariant under translations, dilations and hyperbolic rotations; reflections flip the curvature sign.

nodes.name: Elastica curvature ODE
nodes.statement: -\kappa''+\kappa =\frac{1}{2}\kappa^3,\qquad\quad \mu := -(\kappa')^2+ \kappa^2 - \frac{1}{4}\kappa^4 \in\mathbb{R}.
nodes.section: 3 Classification of elasticae in the hyperbolic plane
nodes.origin_citation: Langer & Singer 1984 (the total squared curvature)
nodes.label: eq:ODE_kappa

nodes.name: Classification of curvature functions of elasticae in H
nodes.statement:
From Table (2.7)(c) in~\cite{LanSing_the_total} for $G=-1$ we find
  that $\kappa$ is, up to multiplication by $-1$, one of the following functions:
  \begin{align*}
	&(i)\;\;\quad \kappa\equiv \sqrt{2} &&\mu = 1\\
	&(ii)\;\quad \kappa(s) =  \frac{2}{\sqrt{2-k^2}}\mathrm{dn}\Big(\frac{s+a}{\sqrt{2-k^2}},k\Big)\quad(0<k<1)
	&& \mu =\frac{4(1-k^2)}{(2-k^2)^2}, \\ 
	&(iii)\quad \kappa\equiv 0 \quad\text{or}\quad \kappa(s)= 2\mathrm{sech}(s+a) &&\mu= 0, \\
	&(iv)\;\quad \kappa(s)= \frac{2k}{\sqrt{2k^2-1}} \mathrm{cn}\Big(\frac{s+a}{\sqrt{2k^2-1}},k\Big)\quad
	  (\frac{1}{\sqrt 2}<k<1)
	  && \mu = - \frac{4k^2(1-k^2)}{(2k^2-1)^2}.
  \end{align*}
nodes.section: 3 Classification of elasticae in the hyperbolic plane
nodes.origin_citation: Langer & Singer 1984 (the total squared curvature)
conclusions: $\kappa$ is, up to multiplication by $-1$, one of the following functions:
nodes.statement_short: Up to sign, elastica curvatures are constant sqrt2, a scaled dn-function, 0 or 2 sech, or a scaled cn-function.

nodes.name: circular, orbitlike, geodesic and wavelike elasticae
nodes.statement:
These figures motivate the names (i) circular, (ii) orbitlike, (iii)
  geodesic / asymptotically geodesic or (iv) wavelike, respectively.
nodes.section: 3 Classification of elasticae in the hyperbolic plane

nodes.name: distance function Z
nodes.statement:
The key to achieve this goal
   is a thorough discussion of the function 
  \begin{equation} Z(s;P) = \frac{(\gamma_1(s)-P_1)^2+(\gamma_2(s)-P_2)^2}{2P_2\gamma_2(s)} \qquad\text{for all }
    P=(P_1,P_2)\in 
    \mathbb{C} \text{ with }P_2\neq 0,
  \end{equation}
  which for $P\in\mathbb{H}$  is a conformal invariant due to $d_{\mathbb{H}}(\gamma(s),P) = \mathrm{Arcosh}(1+Z(s;P))$,
  see~\eqref{eq:metric}.
nodes.section: 3 Classification of elasticae in the hyperbolic plane
nodes.statement_short: Z(s;P) measures the (conformally invariant) hyperbolic distance of gamma(s) to a point P.

nodes.name: Definition of Z(s;P)
nodes.statement: Z(s;P) = \frac{(\gamma_1(s)-P_1)^2+(\gamma_2(s)-P_2)^2}{2P_2\gamma_2(s)} \qquad\text{for all } P=(P_1,P_2)\in \mathbb{C} \text{ with }P_2\neq 0,
nodes.section: 3 Classification of elasticae in the hyperbolic plane
nodes.label: eq:def_Z

nodes.name: Willmore Conjecture
nodes.statement:
Notably the Willmore Conjecture says that the infimum of the Willmore energy in
  the class of immersed tori in $\mathbb{R}^3$ is achieved by the Clifford-Torus.
nodes.section: 3 Classification of elasticae in the hyperbolic plane
nodes.origin_citation: Marques & Neves
assumptions: in the class of immersed tori in $\mathbb{R}^3$
conclusions: the infimum of the Willmore energy in the class of immersed tori in $\mathbb{R}^3$ is achieved by the Clifford-Torus

nodes.name: Explicit parametrization of the Clifford torus
nodes.statement:
One explicit parametrization of the Clifford torus is given by
	\begin{align*}
 	  \gamma(s) = \Big( \frac{(1+\sqrt{2})\sin(s)}{\sqrt{2}+\cos(s)},
 	  \frac{1+\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{2}+\cos(s)}\Big),\quad
 	  e^{i\phi(s)} =  \frac{1+\sqrt{2}\cos(s)+i\cdot \sin(s)}{\sqrt{2}+\cos(s)}.
	\end{align*}
  This precise realization of the Clifford torus corresponds to solving \eqref{eq:ODE_solution} for
  $\gamma(0)=(0,1),\phi(0)=0$ and $\kappa\equiv \sqrt{2}$.
nodes.section: 3 Classification of elasticae in the hyperbolic plane

nodes.name: Explicit geodesics in H
nodes.statement:
If $\phi(0)\in (\pm \frac{\pi}{2}+2\pi)\mathbb{Z}$ then the geodesic through $(0,1)$ is vertical and given by
  $\gamma(s)=(0,e^{\pm s}),\phi(s)=\phi(0)$.
  Otherwise, for instance in case $\phi(0)=0$, we find the halfcircles 
  $$
     \gamma(s) = (\tanh(s),\mathrm{sech}(s)),\qquad e^{i\phi(s)}= \mathrm{sech}(s) - i\cdot \tanh(s).
   $$
nodes.section: 3 Classification of elasticae in the hyperbolic plane

nodes.name: Asymptotically geodesic elastica (catenoid)
nodes.statement:
The third exceptional family of elasticae is the asymptotically geodesic one which corresponds to the
   conformal class of the catenoid. By definition, it is the graph of the $\cosh$-function and therefore   
   $$
      \gamma(s) = (s,\cosh(s)),\qquad 
      e^{i\phi(s)} = \mathrm{sech}(s)+i\cdot \tanh(s).  
   $$
nodes.section: 3 Classification of elasticae in the hyperbolic plane

nodes.name: Linear ODE for the distance function Z
nodes.statement: Let $\gamma:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{H}$ be parametrized by hyperbolic arclength and $Z$ be given by \eqref{eq:def_Z}. Then, for all $P\in \mathbb{C}^2$ with $P_2\neq 0$, the function $Z(\cdot;P)$ satisfies \begin{equation} \kappa Z''-2\kappa'Z'+\kappa(Z+1)\equiv 2\mu C \end{equation} where $C\in\mathbb{C}$ is, for any $s_0\in\mathbb{R}$, given by \begin{align} \begin{aligned} C &= \frac{P_2^2+(\gamma_1(s_0)-P_1)^2}{2P_2\gamma_2(s_0)}\cdot\Big(\frac{\kappa(s_0)}{\mu}+\frac{\kappa'(s_0)}{\mu}\sin(\phi(s_0)) - \frac{\kappa(s_0)^2}{2\mu}\cos(\phi(s_0))\Big) \\ & + \frac{\gamma_2(s_0)}{2P_2}\cdot \Big(\frac{\kappa(s_0)}{\mu}-\frac{\kappa'(s_0)}{\mu}\sin(\phi(s_0)) + \frac{\kappa(s_0)^2}{2\mu}\cos(\phi(s_0))\Big) \\ &+ \frac{\gamma_1(s_0)-P_1}{P_2}\cdot \Big( -\frac{\kappa(s_0)^2}{2\mu}\sin(\phi(s_0))-\frac{\kappa'(s_0)}{\mu}\cos(\phi(s_0)) \Big). \end{aligned} \end{align}
nodes.section: 3 Classification of elasticae in the hyperbolic plane
assumptions: Let $\gamma:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{H}$ be parametrized by hyperbolic arclength and $Z$ be given by \eqref{eq:def_Z}.
conclusions: the function $Z(\cdot;P)$ satisfies
nodes.statement_short: Along an elastica, Z(.;P) solves the second-order linear ODE kappa Z'' - 2 kappa' Z' + kappa(Z+1) = 2 mu C with explicit constant C.
nodes.label: prop:ode_Z

nodes.name: ODE for Z
nodes.statement: \kappa Z''-2\kappa'Z'+\kappa(Z+1)\equiv 2\mu C
nodes.section: 3 Classification of elasticae in the hyperbolic plane
nodes.label: eq:ODE_Z

nodes.name: Formula for the constant C
nodes.statement: \begin{aligned} C &= \frac{P_2^2+(\gamma_1(s_0)-P_1)^2}{2P_2\gamma_2(s_0)}\cdot\Big(\frac{\kappa(s_0)}{\mu}+\frac{\kappa'(s_0)}{\mu}\sin(\phi(s_0)) - \frac{\kappa(s_0)^2}{2\mu}\cos(\phi(s_0))\Big) \\ & + \frac{\gamma_2(s_0)}{2P_2}\cdot \Big(\frac{\kappa(s_0)}{\mu}-\frac{\kappa'(s_0)}{\mu}\sin(\phi(s_0)) + \frac{\kappa(s_0)^2}{2\mu}\cos(\phi(s_0))\Big) \\ &+ \frac{\gamma_1(s_0)-P_1}{P_2}\cdot \Big( -\frac{\kappa(s_0)^2}{2\mu}\sin(\phi(s_0))-\frac{\kappa'(s_0)}{\mu}\cos(\phi(s_0)) \Big). \end{aligned}
nodes.section: 3 Classification of elasticae in the hyperbolic plane
nodes.label: eq:def_C

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 1
nodes.statement: For convenience we write $Z:=Z(\cdot;P)$. Differentiating $Z$ gives the formula \begin{equation} Z' = \frac{\gamma_1-P_1}{P_2} \cdot \cos(\phi) + \frac{\gamma_2^2-P_2^2-(\gamma_1-P_1)^2}{2P_2\gamma_2}\cdot \sin(\phi). \end{equation} Differentiating once more and using $\phi'+\cos(\phi)=\kappa$ gives \begin{align*} Z'' &= \phi'\cdot \Big( - \frac{\gamma_1-P_1}{P_2}\cdot \sin(\phi) + \frac{\gamma_2^2-P_2^2-(\gamma_1-P_1)^2}{2P_2\gamma_2}\cdot\cos(\phi) \Big) \\ &\quad + \frac{\gamma_1'}{P_2}\cos(\phi) + \frac{2\gamma_2^2\gamma_2'-2(\gamma_1-P_1)\gamma_2\gamma_1' - (\gamma_2^2-P_2^2-(\gamma_1-P_1)^2)\gamma_2' }{2P_2\gamma_2^2} \sin(\phi) \\ &= (\kappa-\cos(\phi)) \cdot \Big( - \frac{\gamma_1-P_1}{P_2}\cdot \sin(\phi) + \frac{\gamma_2^2-P_2^2-(\gamma_1-P_1)^2}{2P_2\gamma_2}\cdot\cos(\phi) \Big) \\ &\quad + \frac{\gamma_2}{P_2}\cdot \cos^2(\phi) + \frac{(\gamma_2^2+P_2^2+ (\gamma_1-P_1)^2) \sin(\phi) -2(\gamma_1-P_1)\gamma_2\cos(\phi)}{2P_2\gamma_2} \cdot \sin(\phi) \\ &= (\kappa-\cos(\phi)) \cdot \Big( - \frac{\gamma_1-P_1}{P_2}\cdot \sin(\phi) + \frac{\gamma_2^2-P_2^2-(\gamma_1-P_1)^2}{2P_2\gamma_2}\cdot\cos(\phi) \Big) \\ &\quad + \frac{\gamma_2}{P_2}\cdot \cos^2(\phi) + \frac{\gamma_2^2+P_2^2+(\gamma_1-P_1)^2}{2P_2\gamma_2} \cdot \sin^2(\phi) -\frac{\gamma_1-P_1}{P_2}\cdot \sin(\phi)\cos(\phi) \\ &= \frac{\gamma_2^2+P_2^2+(\gamma_1-P_1)^2}{2P_2\gamma_2} - \kappa w \\ &= Z+1-\kappa w. \end{align*} Here, the auxiliary function $w$ is given by $$ w : = \frac{\gamma_1-P_1}{P_2} \cdot \sin(\phi) - \frac{\gamma_2^2-P_2^2-(\gamma_1-P_1)^2}{2P_2\gamma_2} \cdot \cos(\phi). $$ From the identity \begin{align*} w' &= \Big(\frac{\gamma_1-P_1}{P_2} \cdot \cos(\phi) + \frac{\gamma_2^2-P_2^2-(\gamma_1-P_1)^2}{2P_2\gamma_2}\cdot \sin(\phi) \Big) \phi' \\ &\;+ \Big( \frac{\gamma_2}{P_2}\cdot \sin(\phi) - \Big(\frac{\gamma_2^2-P_2^2-(\gamma_1-P_1)^2}{2P_2\gamma_2}\Big)'\Big) \cdot \cos(\phi) \\ &= \Big(\frac{\gamma_1-P_1}{P_2} \cdot \cos(\phi) + \frac{\gamma_2^2-P_2^2-(\gamma_1-P_1)^2}{2P_2\gamma_2}\cdot \sin(\phi) \Big) \phi' \\ &\;+ \Big(\frac{\gamma_1-P_1}{P_2} \cdot \cos(\phi) + \frac{\gamma_2^2-P_2^2-(\gamma_1-P_1)^2}{2P_2\gamma_2}\cdot \sin(\phi) \Big) \cos(\phi) \\ &= Z' (\phi'+\cos(\phi)) \\ &= \kappa Z' \end{align*} we get \begin{align*} (\kappa Z''-2\kappa'Z'+\kappa Z + \kappa)' &= (-\kappa^2 w-2\kappa'Z'+ 2\kappa Z + 2\kappa)' \\ &= Z'(-2\kappa''+2\kappa) -2\kappa^2w' + 2\kappa' (- \kappa w -Z'' + Z+1) \\ &\stackrel{\eqref{eq:ODE_kappa}}{=} Z'(-2\kappa''+2\kappa-\kappa^3) \\ &= 0 \end{align*} so that $\kappa Z''-2\kappa'Z'+\kappa Z + \kappa$ must be constant. If we define $C\in\mathbb{C}$ to be the complex number with $\kappa Z''-2\kappa'Z'+\kappa Z + \kappa\equiv 2\mu C$, then we finally find for all $s_0\in\mathbb{R}$ \begin{align*} 2\mu C &= \kappa(s_0) Z''(s_0)-2\kappa'(s_0)Z'(s_0)+\kappa(s_0)(Z(s_0)+1) \\ &= 2\kappa(s_0) (Z(s_0)+1) -\kappa(s_0)^2 w(s_0) -2\kappa'(s_0)Z'(s_0) \\ &= \frac{P_2^2+(\gamma_1(s_0)-P_1)^2}{2P_2\gamma_2(s_0)}\cdot\Big(2\kappa(s_0) +2\kappa'(s_0) \sin(\phi(s_0)) - \kappa(s_0)^2 \cos(\phi(s_0))\Big) \\ & + \frac{\gamma_2(s_0)}{2P_2}\cdot \Big(2\kappa(s_0) -2\kappa'(s_0) \sin(\phi(s_0)) + \kappa(s_0)^2 \cos(\phi(s_0))\Big) \\ &+ \frac{\gamma_1(s_0)-P_1}{P_2}\cdot \Big( - \kappa(s_0)^2 \sin(\phi(s_0))-2\kappa'(s_0) \cos(\phi(s_0)) \Big). \end{align*}
nodes.section: 3 Classification of elasticae in the hyperbolic plane
nodes.statement_short: Differentiate Z twice using the ODE system and the elastica equation; the combination kappa Z''-2kappa'Z'+kappa(Z+1) has zero derivative.

nodes.name: Formula for Z'
nodes.statement: Z' = \frac{\gamma_1-P_1}{P_2} \cdot \cos(\phi) + \frac{\gamma_2^2-P_2^2-(\gamma_1-P_1)^2}{2P_2\gamma_2}\cdot \sin(\phi).
nodes.section: 3 Classification of elasticae in the hyperbolic plane
nodes.label: eq:formula_Zprime

nodes.name: Fourth-order ODE for Z and Euclidean analogue
nodes.statement: ~ \begin{itemize} \item[(a)] Differentiating \eqref{eq:ODE_Z} twice one finds $2Z^{(iv)} + \big((3\kappa^2-4)Z'\big)' + (2-\kappa^2)(Z+1) =0$. This ODE is, in contrast to \eqref{eq:ODE_Z}, not singular at zeros of $\kappa$. In particular $Z$ is smooth even in the wavelike case where $\kappa$ has infinitely many zeros. Since we will not make use of this ODE we omit the proof. \item[(b)] A similar result may be shown for elastic curves in the Euclidean plane that have recently been studied in \cite{DecGru_bvp,Man_bvp}. Such curves $\hat\gamma$, now parametrized by Euclidean arclength with curvature $\hat\kappa$, satisfy $\hat \kappa \hat Z''-2\hat\kappa'\hat Z'= const$ where $\hat Z(s):= (\gamma_1(s)-P_1)^2+(\gamma_2(s)-P_2)^2$. \end{itemize}
nodes.section: 3 Classification of elasticae in the hyperbolic plane
nodes.statement_short: Z satisfies a nonsingular fourth-order ODE (proof omitted); an analogous identity holds for Euclidean elastic curves.

nodes.name: elliptic integrals of the first and second kind
nodes.statement:
The elliptic integrals of the first and second kind are defined by 
    $$
      F(l,k) := \int_0^l \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-t^2}\sqrt{1-k^2t^2}}\,dt, \qquad
      E(l,k) := \int_0^l \frac{\sqrt{1-k^2t^2}}{\sqrt{1-t^2}}\,dt
    $$
    and in the special case $l=1$ we obtain the so-called complete elliptic integrals
    $K(k) := F(1,k)$, $E(k) := E(1,k)$.
nodes.origin_citation: Byrd & Friedman, Handbook of elliptic integrals

nodes.name: Derivatives of complete elliptic integrals
nodes.statement: K'(k) = \frac{E(k)-(1-k^2)K(k)}{k(1-k^2)},\qquad E'(k) = \frac{E(k)-K(k)}{k}.
nodes.origin_citation: Byrd & Friedman, Handbook of elliptic integrals
nodes.label: eq:derivative_EK

nodes.name: Jacobi elliptic functions sn, cn, dn
nodes.statement:
As we will see in \eqref{eq:Jac_Inverse} these functions relate to Jacobi's elliptic functions
    $\mathrm{sn}(\cdot,k),\mathrm{cn}(\cdot,k),\mathrm{dn}(\cdot,k)$ (we omit the arguments for convenience) that can be defined as
    the unique solution of the initial value problem
    \begin{align} \mathrm{sn}' = \mathrm{cn}\mathrm{dn}, \quad
      \mathrm{cn}'=-\mathrm{sn}\mathrm{dn},\quad
      \mathrm{dn}' = -k^2\mathrm{sn}\mathrm{cn},\quad
      \mathrm{sn}(0)=0,\;\mathrm{cn}(0)=\mathrm{dn}(0)=1. 
    \end{align}
nodes.origin_citation: Byrd & Friedman, Handbook of elliptic integrals

nodes.name: Initial value problem defining sn, cn, dn
nodes.statement: \mathrm{sn}' = \mathrm{cn}\mathrm{dn}, \quad \mathrm{cn}'=-\mathrm{sn}\mathrm{dn},\quad \mathrm{dn}' = -k^2\mathrm{sn}\mathrm{cn},\quad \mathrm{sn}(0)=0,\;\mathrm{cn}(0)=\mathrm{dn}(0)=1.
nodes.origin_citation: Byrd & Friedman, Handbook of elliptic integrals
nodes.label: eq:Jacobi_ODE_1terOrdnung

nodes.name: Pythagorean identities for Jacobi functions
nodes.statement: \mathrm{cn}^2+\mathrm{sn}^2 = 1,\qquad \mathrm{dn}^2+k^2\mathrm{sn}^2 = 1,
nodes.origin_citation: Byrd & Friedman, Handbook of elliptic integrals
nodes.label: eq:Jacobi_trigonometric_identities

nodes.name: Second-order ODEs for Jacobi functions
nodes.statement: \mathrm{cn}'' = (2k^2-1)\mathrm{cn} -2k^2\mathrm{cn}^3, \; \mathrm{sn}'' = -(1+k^2)\mathrm{sn} +2k^2\mathrm{sn}^3,\; \mathrm{dn}'' = (2-k^2)\mathrm{dn} -2\mathrm{dn}^3.
nodes.origin_citation: Byrd & Friedman, Handbook of elliptic integrals
nodes.label: eq:Jacobi_ODE_2terOrdnung

nodes.name: Inverses of Jacobi functions
nodes.statement: \mathrm{sn}^{-1}(z,k) = F(z,k),\quad \mathrm{cn}^{-1}(z,k) = F(\sqrt{1-z^2},k),\quad \mathrm{dn}^{-1}(z,k) = F(\sqrt{1-z^2}/k,k).
nodes.origin_citation: Byrd & Friedman, Handbook of elliptic integrals
nodes.label: eq:Jac_Inverse

nodes.name: Addition formulas for shift by K(k)
nodes.statement: \mathrm{cn}(s-K(k)) = \sqrt{1-k^2} \frac{\mathrm{sn}(s)}{\mathrm{dn}(s)},\; \mathrm{sn}(s-K(k)) = -\frac{\mathrm{cn}(s)}{\mathrm{dn}(s)},\; \mathrm{dn}(s-K(k)) = \frac{\sqrt{1-k^2}}{\mathrm{dn}(s)},
nodes.origin_citation: Byrd & Friedman, Handbook of elliptic integrals
nodes.label: eq:Jac_Additionstheoreme

nodes.name: Heuman's Lambda function
nodes.statement:
Next we define Heuman's Lambda function  $\Lambda_0$ via
    $$
      \Lambda_0(\arcsin(l),k):=\frac{2}{\pi} (E(k)F(l,k')+K(k)E(l,k')-K(k)F(l,k')),
    $$
    see 150.03 in \cite{ByrFri_handbook}.
nodes.origin_citation: Byrd & Friedman, Handbook of elliptic integrals

nodes.name: complementary modulus k'
nodes.statement: Here and in the text we will write $k':=\sqrt{1-k^2}$.

nodes.name: Derivatives of Heuman's Lambda function
nodes.statement: \begin{aligned} \frac{\partial}{\partial l} \Lambda_0(\arcsin(l),k) &= \frac{2(E(k)-(1-k^2)l^2K(k))}{\pi l'\sqrt{1-(1-k^2)l^2}},\\ \frac{\partial}{\partial k} \Lambda_0(\arcsin(l),k) &= \frac{2(E(k)-K(k))ll'}{\pi k\sqrt{1-(1-k^2)l^2}}. \end{aligned}
nodes.origin_citation: Byrd & Friedman, Handbook of elliptic integrals
nodes.label: eq:derivative_Heuman

nodes.name: Jacobi eta, theta and zeta functions
nodes.statement:
Additionally, we will need Jacobi's eta, theta and zeta functions
    $H,\Theta,\Theta_1,\zeta:\mathbb{C}\times(0,1)\to\mathbb{C}$ defined through the following formulas (see 144.01 and 
    1050.01 in \cite{ByrFri_handbook}):
    \begin{align*}
      &\Theta(z,k) := \vartheta_0(\frac{\pi z}{2 K(k)},q_k),
      &&H(z,k) := \vartheta_1(\frac{\pi z}{2 K(k)},q_k),  \\
      &\Theta_1(z,k) := \vartheta_3(\frac{\pi z}{2 K(k)},q_k), 
      &&\zeta(z,k) := \frac{\Theta_z(z,k)}{\Theta(z,k)}. 
    \end{align*}
nodes.origin_citation: Byrd & Friedman, Handbook of elliptic integrals

nodes.name: Jacobian theta functions and elliptic nome
nodes.statement:
Here, the Jacobian Theta Functions $\vartheta_0,\vartheta_1$ and the elliptic nome $q_k$ are given by
    \begin{align} \begin{aligned}
      \vartheta_0(z,q)
      &= 1 + 2 \sum_{n=1}^\infty (-1)^n q^{n^2}\cos(2nz), \\
      \vartheta_1(z,q)
      &= 2   \sum_{n=0}^\infty (-1)^n q^{(n+1/2)^2}\sin((2n+1)z), \\


      \vartheta_3(z,q)
      &= 1 + 2\sum_{n=1}^\infty q^{n^2}\cos(2nz), \\
      q_k  
      &= \exp(-\pi K(k')/K(k)).
       
       
       \end{aligned}
    \end{align}
nodes.origin_citation: Byrd & Friedman, Handbook of elliptic integrals

nodes.name: Series of Jacobian theta functions
nodes.statement: \begin{aligned} \vartheta_0(z,q) &= 1 + 2 \sum_{n=1}^\infty (-1)^n q^{n^2}\cos(2nz), \\ \vartheta_1(z,q) &= 2 \sum_{n=0}^\infty (-1)^n q^{(n+1/2)^2}\sin((2n+1)z), \\ \vartheta_3(z,q) &= 1 + 2\sum_{n=1}^\infty q^{n^2}\cos(2nz), \\ q_k &= \exp(-\pi K(k')/K(k)). \end{aligned}
nodes.origin_citation: Byrd & Friedman, Handbook of elliptic integrals
nodes.label: eq:JacobianTheta_series

nodes.name: curvature function of an orbitlike elastica
nodes.statement:
So from now on let
    always $\gamma:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{H}$ denote an orbitlike elastica with (hyperbolic)  curvature function
    \begin{equation} \kappa(s)=\frac{2}{\sqrt{2-k^2}}\mathrm{dn}(\frac{s+s_*}{\sqrt{2-k^2}},k)
    \end{equation}
    for $0<k<1,s_*\in\mathbb{R}$ and let $\phi,Z$ be defined as in \eqref{eq:ODE_solution},\eqref{eq:def_Z}.
nodes.statement_short: Throughout, gamma is an orbitlike elastica with curvature a rescaled, shifted dn-function with modulus k.

nodes.name: Orbitlike curvature function
nodes.statement: \kappa(s)=\frac{2}{\sqrt{2-k^2}}\mathrm{dn}(\frac{s+s_*}{\sqrt{2-k^2}},k)
nodes.label: eq:def_kappa_orbitlike

nodes.name: rotation Delta theta_k
nodes.statement:
In order to measure the angular progress of an elastica generated by this
    curvature function via \eqref{eq:ODE_solution} we will need





   \begin{equation} \Delta\theta_k := \pi- \pi \Lambda_0(\arcsin(k'),k)  + 2\sqrt{1-k^2}\sqrt{2-k^2}K(k),
   \end{equation}
   a function that has been introduced and analyzed in Proposition 5.3 in~\cite{LanSing_the_total}.
nodes.origin_citation: Langer & Singer 1984 (the total squared curvature)

nodes.name: Definition of Delta theta_k
nodes.statement: \Delta\theta_k := \pi- \pi \Lambda_0(\arcsin(k'),k) + 2\sqrt{1-k^2}\sqrt{2-k^2}K(k),
nodes.label: eq:def_rotation

nodes.name: Discrepancy in Langer-Singer's formulas for Delta theta_k
nodes.statement:
We mention that Langer and Singer gave two expressions for $\Delta\theta_k$ on page 21 in
   \cite{LanSing_the_total} which, however, do not coincide. We chose the correct second expression
   as a definition. In their first expression the factor $(1-p^2)$ has to replaced by
   $\sqrt{1-p^2}$, as we will see in the proof of Proposition~\ref{prop:properties_vartheta_orbitlike}.

nodes.name: Fundamental system of the Lame-type equation (orbitlike)
nodes.statement: For all $k\in (0,1)$ the ordinary differential equation $w''+2\mathrm{dn}^2(\cdot,k)w=0$ has a fundamental system $\{w_1,w_2\}$ on $\mathbb{R}$ such that the following holds: \begin{itemize} \item[(i)] $w_1$ is odd about 0, $w_2$ is even about 0, $w_2(0)>0>w_1'(0)$, \item[(ii)] $w_1(s)^2+w_2(s)^2=2-k^2 -\mathrm{dn}^2(s,k)$ on $\mathbb{R}$, \item[(iii)] $w_1(s)w_1'(s)+w_2(s)w_2'(s) = k^2\mathrm{dn}(s,k)\mathrm{cn}(s,k)\mathrm{sn}(s,k)$ on $\mathbb{R}$, \item[(iv)] $w_1(s)w_2'(s)-w_2(s)w_1'(s) = \sqrt{1-k^2}\sqrt{2-k^2}$ on $\mathbb{R}$, \item[(v)] $(w_1+iw_2)(s+2lK(k)) = (w_1+iw_2)(s) e^{il\Delta\theta_k}$ for all $s\in\mathbb{R},l\in\mathbb{Z}$, \item[(vi)] $(w_1+iw_2)(-K(k)) = e^{i(\pi-\Delta\theta_k)/2}$. \end{itemize}
conclusions: the ordinary differential equation $w''+2\mathrm{dn}^2(\cdot,k)w=0$ has a fundamental system $\{w_1,w_2\}$ on $\mathbb{R}$ such that the following holds:
nodes.statement_short: w''+2dn^2 w=0 has a fundamental system w1,w2 with explicit parity, norm, Wronskian and quasi-periodicity e^{i Delta theta_k}.
nodes.label: prop:w1w2_orbitlike

nodes.name: Relation to the Lame equation
nodes.statement:
We remark that the equation $w''+2\mathrm{dn}^2(\cdot,k)w=0$ is a special case ($h=2,n=1$) of the so-called
   Lam\'{e} equation which is typically written in the form $w''=(n(n+1)k^2\mathrm{sn}^2(\cdot,k)-h)w$, where $h$ is
   called the Lam\'{e} eigenvalue.

nodes.name: rescaled functions W_j (orbitlike)
nodes.statement:
Now, being
   given $w_1,w_2$ we define
   \begin{align} W_j(s) := \frac{1}{\sqrt{2-k^2}} w_j\big(-K(k)+ \frac{s+s_*}{\sqrt{2-k^2}}\big) \qquad (j=1,2).
     
   \end{align}

nodes.name: Definition of W_j
nodes.statement: W_j(s) := \frac{1}{\sqrt{2-k^2}} w_j\big(-K(k)+ \frac{s+s_*}{\sqrt{2-k^2}}\big) \qquad (j=1,2).
nodes.label: eq:def_Wj

nodes.name: Identities for W_1, W_2 (orbitlike)
nodes.statement: Let $\kappa$ be given by \eqref{eq:def_kappa_orbitlike}. Then $\{W_1,W_2\}$ is a fundamental system of the ODE $W''+2\mu\kappa^{-2}W=0$ and the following identities hold on $\mathbb{R}$: \begin{itemize} \item[(i)] $W_1^2+W_2^2 = \frac{\kappa^2-\mu}{\kappa^2}$, \item[(ii)] $W_1'= \frac{\mu \kappa'}{\kappa(\kappa^2-\mu)} W_1 - \frac{\sqrt\mu \kappa^2}{2(\kappa^2-\mu)}W_2 $, \item[(iii)] $W_2' = \frac{\sqrt\mu \kappa^2}{2(\kappa^2-\mu)}W_1 + \frac{\mu \kappa'}{\kappa(\kappa^2-\mu)} W_2$, \item[(iv)] $W_1W_2'-W_2W_1' = \frac{\sqrt{\mu}}{2}$, \item[(v)] $(W_1+iW_2)(s+2l\sqrt{2-k^2}K(k))=(W_1+iW_2)(s)e^{il\Delta\theta_k}$ for $s\in\mathbb{R},l\in\mathbb{Z}$, \item[(vi)] $(W_1+iW_2)(s)= (-W_1+iW_2)(-s-2s_*+2l\sqrt{2-k^2}K(k)) e^{i(l-1)\Delta\theta_k}$ for $s\in\mathbb{R},l\in\mathbb{Z}$. \end{itemize}
conclusions: $\{W_1,W_2\}$ is a fundamental system of the ODE $W''+2\mu\kappa^{-2}W=0$ and the following identities hold on $\mathbb{R}$:
nodes.statement_short: W1,W2 solve W''+2mu kappa^{-2} W=0 and satisfy explicit norm, derivative, Wronskian, periodicity and reflection identities.
nodes.label: prop:W1W2_orbitlike

nodes.name: angle function vartheta (orbitlike)
nodes.statement:
Next we choose an angle function $\vartheta$ as follows:
  \begin{align} W_2(s)-iW_1(s) = \frac{
                     \sqrt{\kappa^2-\mu}}{\kappa} e^{i\vartheta(s)}.
  \end{align}
  This definition makes sense due to Proposition~\ref{prop:W1W2_orbitlike}~(i).
  Notice that \eqref{eq:def_theta} determines $\vartheta$ only up to additive multiples of $2\pi$ so that we
  require $\vartheta$ to satisfy the inequality $-2\pi<\vartheta(-s_*)\leq 0$.

nodes.name: Definition of vartheta
nodes.statement: W_2(s)-iW_1(s) = \frac{ \sqrt{\kappa^2-\mu}}{\kappa} e^{i\vartheta(s)}.
nodes.label: eq:def_theta

nodes.name: Properties of vartheta (orbitlike)
nodes.statement: The following identities hold: $$ \vartheta' = \frac{\sqrt\mu \kappa^2}{2(\kappa^2-\mu)},\qquad \matII{W_1}{W_2}{W_1'}{W_2'} = \matII{0}{\frac{\sqrt{\kappa^2-\mu}}{\kappa}}{\frac{-\sqrt{\mu}\kappa}{2\sqrt{\kappa^2-\mu}}}{ \frac{\mu\kappa'}{\kappa^2\sqrt{\kappa^2-\mu}}} \matII{\cos(\vartheta)}{\sin(\vartheta)}{-\sin(\vartheta)}{\cos(\vartheta)}. $$ Moreover, we have for $s\in\mathbb{R},l\in\mathbb{Z}$ \begin{itemize} \item[(i)] $\vartheta(-s_*+l\sqrt{2-k^2}K(k)) = \frac{l-1}{2}\Delta\theta_k$, \item[(ii)] $\vartheta(s+2l\sqrt{2-k^2}K(k))-\vartheta(s) = l\Delta\theta_k$, \item[(iii)] $\vartheta(-s_*+s)+\vartheta(-s_*-s) = -\Delta\theta_k$. \end{itemize}
conclusions: The following identities hold:
nodes.statement_short: vartheta' = sqrt(mu) kappa^2/(2(kappa^2-mu)), W is a rotation of an explicit matrix, and vartheta advances by Delta theta_k per period.
nodes.label: prop:properties_vartheta_orbitlike

nodes.name: auxiliary vectors xi^1, xi^2, xi^3
Definition of xi^1, xi^2, xi^3
nodes.statement: \begin{aligned} \xi^1(s) &:= \matII{ W_1(s)}{W_2(s)}{ W_1'(s)}{ W_2'(s)}^{-1} \vecII{\frac{1}{\kappa(s)}-\frac{\kappa(s)}{\mu}-\frac{\kappa'(s)}{\mu}\sin(\phi(s)) +\frac{\kappa(s)^2}{2\mu}\cos(\phi(s))}{-\frac{1}{\kappa(s)}\sin(\phi(s))-\frac{\kappa'(s)}{\kappa(s)^2}}, \\ \xi^2(s) &:= \matII{ W_1(s)}{ W_2(s)}{ W_1'(s)}{ W_2'(s)}^{-1} \vecII{\frac{1}{\kappa(s)}-\frac{\kappa(s)}{\mu}+\frac{\kappa'(s)}{\mu}\sin(\phi(s)) -\frac{\kappa(s)^2}{2\mu}\cos(\phi(s))}{\frac{1}{\kappa(s)}\sin(\phi(s))-\frac{\kappa'(s)}{\kappa(s)^2}}, \\ \xi^3(s) &:= \matII{ W_1(s)}{ W_2(s)}{ W_1'(s)}{ W_2'(s)}^{-1} \vecII{\frac{\kappa(s)^2}{2\mu}\sin(\phi(s)) +\frac{\kappa'(s)}{\mu}\cos(\phi(s))}{\frac{1}{\kappa(s)}\cos(\phi(s))}. \end{aligned}
nodes.label: eq:formula_xi

nodes.name: Formula for Z (orbitlike)
nodes.statement: For $P=(P_1,P_2)\in\mathbb{R}^2$ such that $P_2\neq 0$ we have \begin{equation} Z(s;P) = -1 + \kappa(s)\big( AW_1(s) + BW_2(s) + C\big) \end{equation} where $C$ is given by \eqref{eq:def_C} and $A,B\in\mathbb{R}$ satisfy \begin{align} \vecII{A}{B} &= \frac{(\gamma_1(s_0)-P_1)^2+P_2^2}{2\gamma_2(s_0)P_2} \xi^1(s_0) + \frac{\gamma_2(s_0)}{2P_2}\xi^2(s_0) + \frac{\gamma_1(s_0)-P_1}{P_2}\xi^3(s_0) \quad\forall s_0\in\mathbb{R}. \end{align}
conclusions: where $C$ is given by \eqref{eq:def_C} and $A,B\in\mathbb{R}$ satisfy
nodes.statement_short: Z(s;P) = -1 + kappa(s)(A W1 + B W2 + C) with A,B given explicitly through xi^1, xi^2, xi^3.
nodes.label: prop:formula_Z_orbitlike

nodes.name: Z = -1 + kappa(A W1 + B W2 + C)
nodes.statement: Z(s;P) = -1 + \kappa(s)\big( AW_1(s) + BW_2(s) + C\big)
nodes.label: eq:formula_Z

nodes.name: Formula for A, B
nodes.statement: \vecII{A}{B} &= \frac{(\gamma_1(s_0)-P_1)^2+P_2^2}{2\gamma_2(s_0)P_2} \xi^1(s_0) + \frac{\gamma_2(s_0)}{2P_2}\xi^2(s_0) + \frac{\gamma_1(s_0)-P_1}{P_2}\xi^3(s_0) \quad\forall s_0\in\mathbb{R}.
nodes.label: eq:formula_AB

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 5
nodes.statement: Let $C$ be given by \eqref{eq:def_C} so that $Z(\cdot;P)$ satisfies the ODE \eqref{eq:ODE_Z}. We define the auxiliary function $W(s) := (Z(s;P)+1)\kappa(s)^{-1}-C$. Then we get \begin{align*} W''(s) &= \frac{1}{\kappa(s)^2} \Big( \kappa(s)Z''(s;P)-2\kappa'(s)Z'(s;P) + (Z(s;P)+1)\big(-\kappa''(s)+2\frac{\kappa'(s)^2}{\kappa(s)}\big) \Big) \\ &\stackrel{\eqref{eq:ODE_Z}}{=} \frac{1}{\kappa(s)^2} \Big( (Z(s;P)+1)\big(-\kappa(s)-\kappa''(s)+2\frac{\kappa'(s)^2}{\kappa(s)} \big) +2\mu C\Big) \\ &\stackrel{\eqref{eq:ODE_kappa}}{=} -\frac{2\mu}{\kappa(s)^2} \Big( \frac{Z(s;P)+1}{\kappa(s)}-C\Big) \\ &= -\frac{2\mu}{\kappa(s)^2}W(s). \end{align*} By Proposition \ref{prop:W1W2_orbitlike} we can find $A,B\in\mathbb{R}$ such that $W(s)=AW_1(s)+BW_2(s)$ and thus \begin{align*} Z(s;P) = -1 + \kappa(s)\big(W(s)+C\big) = -1 + \kappa(s)\big( AW_1(s) + B W_2(s) + C\big) \end{align*} so that \eqref{eq:formula_Z} is proved. Solving this identity for $W_1,W_2$ and differentiating it with respect to~$s$ we get the following equations for $A,B$: \begin{align*} \matII{ W_1(s_0)}{ W_2(s_0)}{ W_1'(s_0)}{ W_2'(s_0)}\vecII{A}{B} = \vecII{\frac{Z(s_0;P)+1}{\kappa(s_0)}-C}{\big(\frac{Z(\cdot;P)+1}{\kappa}-C\big)'(s_0)} = \vecII{\frac{Z(s_0;P)+1}{\kappa(s_0)}-C}{\frac{Z'(s_0;P)}{\kappa(s_0)}- \frac{\kappa'(s_0)(Z(s_0;P)+1)}{\kappa(s_0)^2}}. \end{align*} Plugging in the formulas for $Z(s_0;P),Z'(s_0;P)$ and $C$, see \eqref{eq:def_Z},\eqref{eq:formula_Zprime},\eqref{eq:def_C}.
nodes.statement_short: W=(Z+1)/kappa - C solves the linear ODE of Proposition 3, so it is a combination of W1,W2; solve for A,B at s0.

nodes.name: Explicit formula for orbitlike elasticae
nodes.statement: A curve $\gamma:\mathbb{R}\to \mathbb{H}$ is an orbitlike elastica parametrized by hyperbolic arclength if and only if we have \begin{align} \gamma_1(s) &=\frac{b_1 W_1(s)+b_2 W_2(s)+b_3}{a_1 W_1(s)+a_2 W_2(s)+a_3}, \\ \gamma_2(s) &=\frac{1}{\kappa(s)(a_1 W_1(s)+a_2 W_2(s)+a_3)} \end{align} for $a_1,a_2,a_3,b_1,b_2,b_3\in\mathbb{R}$ such that \begin{equation} a_3= \sqrt{a_1^2+a_2^2}>0,\qquad \vecII{b_1}{b_2} = \frac{b_3}{a_3} \vecII{a_1}{a_2} + \frac{1}{\sqrt{\mu}a_3} \vecII{-a_2}{a_1}. \end{equation} In this case we moreover have for all $s\in\mathbb{R}$ \begin{align} \gamma_2(s)(a_1,a_2)^T&= \xi^1(s) , \\ \gamma_2(s) (b_1,b_2)^T &= \gamma_1(s) \xi^1(s)+ \gamma_2(s) \xi^3(s), \\ \gamma_1(s) &= \frac{b_3}{a_3} +\frac{1}{2\mu a_3}\big(\kappa(s)^2\sin(\phi(s))+2\kappa'(s)\cos(\phi(s))\big), \\ \gamma_2(s) &= \frac{\kappa(s)}{\mu a_3} + \frac{1}{2\mu a_3}\big(2\kappa'(s)\sin(\phi(s))-\kappa(s)^2\cos(\phi(s))\big). \end{align}
conclusions: A curve $\gamma:\mathbb{R}\to \mathbb{H}$ is an orbitlike elastica parametrized by hyperbolic arclength if and only if we have
equivalent_conditions: A curve $\gamma:\mathbb{R}\to \mathbb{H}$ is an orbitlike elastica parametrized by hyperbolic arclength
nodes.statement_short: Orbitlike elasticae are exactly the curves gamma1, gamma2 given as ratios of affine combinations of W1, W2 with coefficients constrained by a3 = |(a1,a2)|.
nodes.label: thm:explicit_formula_orbitlike

nodes.name: Explicit formula for gamma_2 (orbitlike)
nodes.statement: \gamma_2(s) &=\frac{1}{\kappa(s)(a_1 W_1(s)+a_2 W_2(s)+a_3)}
nodes.label: eq:explicit_formula_orbitlike_2

nodes.name: Constraints on the coefficients a_i, b_i
nodes.statement: a_3= \sqrt{a_1^2+a_2^2}>0,\qquad \vecII{b_1}{b_2} = \frac{b_3}{a_3} \vecII{a_1}{a_2} + \frac{1}{\sqrt{\mu}a_3} \vecII{-a_2}{a_1}.
nodes.label: eq:a_1a_2a_3b_1b_2b_3

nodes.name: Identity for (b1,b2)
nodes.statement: \gamma_2(s) (b_1,b_2)^T &= \gamma_1(s) \xi^1(s)+ \gamma_2(s) \xi^3(s),
nodes.label: eq:a1a2b1b2_2

nodes.name: gamma_1 in terms of kappa, phi
nodes.statement: \gamma_1(s) &= \frac{b_3}{a_3} +\frac{1}{2\mu a_3}\big(\kappa(s)^2\sin(\phi(s))+2\kappa'(s)\cos(\phi(s))\big),
nodes.label: eq:b3a3_1

nodes.name: gamma_2 in terms of kappa, phi
nodes.statement: \gamma_2(s) &= \frac{\kappa(s)}{\mu a_3} + \frac{1}{2\mu a_3}\big(2\kappa'(s)\sin(\phi(s))-\kappa(s)^2\cos(\phi(s))\big).
nodes.label: eq:b3a3_2

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 4
nodes.statement_short: Only if: expand Z formula in P and equate coefficients, then compute inner products of xi vectors. If: define phi explicitly and verify the ODE system.

nodes.name: <xi1,xi1> = a3^2 gamma2^2
nodes.label: eq:formulas_scpr_xi_1

nodes.name: <xi1,xi3> identity
nodes.label: eq:formulas_scpr_xi_2

nodes.name: <xi1^perp,xi3> identity
nodes.label: eq:formulas_scpr_xi_3

nodes.name: Definition of phi in the sufficiency proof
nodes.statement: \vecII{\sin(\phi)}{\cos(\phi)} := \frac{\mu a_3}{2(\kappa^2-\mu)}\matII{\kappa^2}{2\kappa'}{2\kappa'}{-\kappa^2} \vecII{\gamma_1-\frac{b_3}{a_3}}{\gamma_2-\frac{\kappa}{\mu a_3}}.
nodes.label: eq:formula_phi

nodes.name: Orbitlike elastica determined by three coefficients
nodes.statement:
Theorem~\ref{thm:explicit_formula_orbitlike} shows that an orbitlike elastica with curvature
       is determined by fixing the three coefficients $a_1,a_2,b_3$. This is not surprising given the fact
       that the solutions of~\eqref{eq:ODE_solution} are uniquely determined by fixing   three initial
       conditions for $\gamma_1,\gamma_2,\phi$.

nodes.name: Derivation of the ball characterization from Z
nodes.statement: From the definition of $Z$ in \eqref{eq:def_Z} we deduce the following:
nodes.statement_short: Direct from the definition of Z.

nodes.name: Z-levels characterize Euclidean balls
nodes.statement:
The inequality
    $Z(s;P)\geq -1+\rho>0$ holds if and only if $\gamma$ lies outside the Euclidean ball with center $(P_1,\rho P_2)$ and
    radius $\sqrt{\rho^2-1}|P_2|$. The same way, we have $Z(s;P)\leq -1+\rho$ if and only if $\gamma$ lies
    inside this ball.
conclusions: $\gamma$ lies outside the Euclidean ball with center $(P_1,\rho P_2)$ and radius $\sqrt{\rho^2-1}|P_2|$
equivalent_conditions: $\gamma$ lies outside the Euclidean ball with center $(P_1,\rho P_2)$ and radius $\sqrt{\rho^2-1}|P_2|$

nodes.name: Hyperbolic circles are Euclidean circles
nodes.statement:
Notice moreover that the above
    reasoning shows  that hyperbolic circles with center $P$ and radius $\mathrm{Arcosh}(\rho)$ are
    nothing but Euclidean balls with center $(P_1,\rho P_2)$ and radius $\sqrt{\rho^2-1}|P_2|$ since both are
    characterized by the identity $Z(s;P)\equiv -1+\rho$, see~\eqref{eq:metric}.
conclusions: hyperbolic circles with center $P$ and radius $\mathrm{Arcosh}(\rho)$ are nothing but Euclidean balls

nodes.name: Choice of P with A=B=0 (orbitlike)
nodes.statement: For $P_1=\frac{b_3}{a_3},P_2=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\mu}a_3}$ we have for all $s\in\mathbb{R}$ $$ Z(s;P) = -1 + \frac{\kappa(s)}{\sqrt\mu}. $$
conclusions: Z(s;P) = -1 +  \frac{\kappa(s)}{\sqrt\mu}.
nodes.label: prop:choice_of_P

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 6
nodes.statement: We will use the notation introduced in the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:explicit_formula_orbitlike}. For the above choice of $P_1,P_2$ we deduce from Theorem~\ref{thm:explicit_formula_orbitlike} and from $\kappa^2|a|^2||W|^2=(\kappa^2-\mu)a_3^2$ \begin{align*} \big(\gamma_1-P_1\big)^2+\big(\gamma_1-P_2\big)^2 &= \Big(\frac{a_3bW-b_3aW}{a_3(aW+a_3)}\Big)^2 + \Big( \frac{(\sqrt\mu-\kappa)a_3-\kappa aW}{\sqrt\mu \kappa a_3(aW+a_3)}\Big)^2 \\ &= \frac{\kappa^2 (a^\perp W)^2 +(\kappa-\sqrt\mu)^2a_3^2 +2\kappa(\kappa-\sqrt\mu)a_3aW + \kappa^2(aW)^2 }{\mu\kappa^2 a_3^2(aW+a_3)^2} \\ &= \frac{\kappa^2 |a|^2|W|^2 +2\kappa(\kappa-\sqrt\mu)a_3aW+(\kappa-\sqrt\mu)^2a_3^2 }{\mu\kappa^2 a_3^2(aW+a_3)^2} \\ &= \frac{2\kappa(\kappa-\sqrt\mu) a_3^2 +2\kappa a_3(\kappa-\sqrt\mu)a_3aW}{\mu\kappa^2 a_3^2(aW+a_3)^2} \\ &= \frac{2}{\sqrt\mu a_3 \kappa(aW+a_3)} \big(-1+\frac{\kappa}{\sqrt\mu}\big) \\ &= 2P_2\gamma_2\big(-1+\frac{\kappa}{\sqrt\mu}\big), \end{align*} which is all we had to show.
nodes.statement_short: Insert the explicit formulas of Theorem 4 and simplify using kappa^2|a|^2|W|^2=(kappa^2-mu)a3^2.

nodes.name: Orbitlike elasticae oscillate between two circles
nodes.statement: We have $\gamma(\mathbb{R})\subset \overline{B_{R_1}(Q_1)}\setminus B_{R_2}(Q_2)$ where \begin{align*} Q_1 &= \Big( \frac{b_3}{a_3},\frac{\sqrt{2+2\sqrt{1-\mu}}}{\mu a_3}\Big),\qquad R_1 = \frac{\sqrt{2-\mu+2\sqrt{1-\mu}}}{\mu a_3}, \\ Q_2 &= \Big( \frac{b_3}{a_3},\frac{\sqrt{2-2\sqrt{1-\mu}}}{\mu a_3}\Big),\qquad R_2 = \frac{\sqrt{2-\mu-2\sqrt{1-\mu}}}{\mu a_3}. \end{align*} The curve $\gamma$ touches $\partial B_{R_1}(Q_1)$ exactly when $\kappa$ attains its maximum and it touches $\partial B_{R_2}(Q_2)$ precisely when $\kappa$ attains its minimum.
conclusions: We have $\gamma(\mathbb{R})\subset \overline{B_{R_1}(Q_1)}\setminus B_{R_2}(Q_2)$
nodes.statement_short: An orbitlike elastica lies in an explicit annulus between two Euclidean circles, touching them at the extrema of kappa.
nodes.label: prop:enclosures

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 7
nodes.statement: We recall $\mu=\frac{4(1-k^2)}{(2-k^2)^2}$ and hence $k^2=\frac{2}{\mu}+\frac{2\sqrt{1-\mu}}{\mu}$. Then, choosing $P=(P_1,P_2)$ as in Proposition \ref{prop:choice_of_P} we obtain the inequalities \begin{align*} Z(s;P) &\leq -1 + \frac{\max \kappa}{\sqrt{\mu}} \stackrel{\eqref{eq:def_kappa_orbitlike}}{=} -1 + \frac{2}{\sqrt{2-k^2}\sqrt\mu} = -1 + \frac{\sqrt{2+2\sqrt{1-\mu}}}{\sqrt{\mu}} =:-1+\rho_1, \\ Z(s;P) &\geq -1 + \frac{\min \kappa}{\sqrt{\mu}} \stackrel{\eqref{eq:def_kappa_orbitlike}}{=} -1 + \frac{2\sqrt{1-k^2}}{\sqrt{2-k^2}\sqrt\mu} = -1 + \frac{\sqrt{2-2\sqrt{1-\mu}}}{\sqrt{\mu}} =: -1+\rho_2. \end{align*} Hence we deduce $\gamma(\mathbb{R})\subset \overline{B_{R_1}(Q_1)}\setminus B_{R_2}(Q_2)$ for $$ Q_1:= (P_1,\rho_1 P_2),\quad Q_2:= (P_1,\rho_2 P_2),\quad R_1:= \sqrt{\rho_1^2-1}|P_2|,\quad R_2:= \sqrt{\rho_2^2-1}|P_2|, $$ which proves the result.
nodes.statement_short: Bound Z(s;P) for the special P of Proposition 6 by max and min of kappa and translate into Euclidean balls.

nodes.name: Monotonicity of Delta theta_k
nodes.statement: The function $k\mapsto \Delta\theta_k$ decreases on $(0,1)$ from its upper limit $\sqrt{2}\pi$ to its lower limit $\pi$.
nodes.origin_citation: Langer & Singer 1984 (the total squared curvature)
conclusions: The function $k\mapsto \Delta\theta_k$ decreases on $(0,1)$ from its upper limit $\sqrt{2}\pi$ to its lower limit $\pi$.
nodes.label: prop:rotation

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 8
nodes.statement: We recall $$ \Delta\theta_k = \pi - \pi\Lambda_0(\arcsin(k'),k)+2\sqrt{1-k^2}\sqrt{2-k^2}K(k). $$ The derivative of this function with respect to $k$ can be computed as follows. From the formulas \eqref{eq:derivative_EK},\eqref{eq:derivative_Heuman} we get \begin{align*} \frac{d}{d k} \big(\Lambda_0(\arcsin(k'),k)\big) &= -\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-k^2}} \frac{2(E(k)-(k')^4K(k))}{\pi\sqrt{1-(k')^4}} + \frac{2(E(k)-K(k))k'}{\pi\sqrt{1-(k')^4}} \\ &= \frac{2}{\pi k'\sqrt{2k^2-k^4}}\big(-E(k)+(k')^4K(k)+(k')^2E(k)-(k')^2K(k)\big) \\ &= -\frac{2k}{\pi k'\sqrt{2-k^2}}(E(k)+(k')^2K(k)), \\ \frac{d}{d k} \big(\sqrt{1-k^2}\sqrt{2-k^2}K(k) \big) &= -\frac{k\sqrt{2-k^2}}{\sqrt{1-k^2}}K(k) -\frac{k\sqrt{1-k^2}}{\sqrt{2-k^2}}K(k) \\ &\; + \sqrt{1-k^2}\sqrt{2-k^2} \frac{E(k)-(k')^2K(k)}{k(k')^2} \\ &= \frac{\sqrt{2-k^2}}{k\sqrt{1-k^2}}E(k) + \frac{k^4-2}{k\sqrt{1-k^2}\sqrt{2-k^2}}K(k). \end{align*} From these identities we get $$ \frac{d}{d k} \big( \Delta\theta_k\big) = \frac{2(2E(k)+(k^2-2)K(k))}{k\sqrt{1-k^2}\sqrt{2-k^2}}, $$ and we have to show that the numerator is negative. In fact, the function $g(k):=2E(k)+(k^2-2)K(k)$ satisfies $g(0)=0$ as well as $g'(k)=k (k')^{-2} (-E(k)+(k')^2K(k))<0$. Indeed, $h(k):=-E(k)+(k')^2K(k)$ satisfies $h(0)=0$ as well as $h'(k)=-kK(k)<0$, see \eqref{eq:derivative_EK} for the formulas for $E'(k),K'(k)$. This proves $h<0$, hence $g'<0,g<0$ on $(0,1)$ and thus the monotonicity of $k\mapsto \Delta\theta_k$. Finally, evaluating $\Delta\theta_k$ for $k=0,k=1$ and using $K(0)=\frac{\pi}{2},\lim_{k\to 1} K(k)\sqrt{1-k^2}=0$ from 112.01 as well as $\Lambda_0(0,1)=0,\Lambda_0(\frac{\pi}{2},0)=1$ from 151.01 in \cite{ByrFri_handbook} we find the values $\sqrt 2 \pi$ respectively $\pi$ so that the claim is proved.
nodes.statement_short: Differentiate Delta theta_k via elliptic-integral derivative formulas and show the numerator 2E+(k^2-2)K is negative.

nodes.name: parameter k_{m,n}
Closedness condition Delta theta_k = 2 pi m/n
nodes.statement: \Delta\theta_k = \frac{2\pi m}{n}
nodes.label: eq:closednedd_condition

nodes.name: closed orbitlike elastica gamma_{m,n}
nodes.statement:
The associated elastica with initial conditions $\gamma_1(0)=0,\gamma_2(0)=1,\phi(0)=0$ and $s_*=0$, say,
 will be denoted by $\gamma_{m,n}$.

nodes.name: hyperbolic length L_{m,n}
nodes.statement:
We now prove that for $k=k_{m,n}$   the
 elastica is closed with hyperbolic length  
 $$
   \mathcal{L}_{m,n}:=2n\sqrt{2-k_{m,n}^2}K(k_{m,n}).
 $$

nodes.name: Closedness and winding number of orbitlike elasticae
nodes.statement: The elastica $\gamma$ is closed if and only if $k=k_{m,n}$ for (w.l.o.g.) coprime integers $m,n\in\mathbb{N}$. In this case $\gamma=\gamma_{m,n}$ closes up after $n$ periods of its curvature function and its winding number around $(P_1,P_2)=(\frac{b_3}{a_3},\frac{1}{\sqrt{\mu}a_3})$ is $m$.
conclusions: The elastica $\gamma$ is closed if and only if $k=k_{m,n}$ for (w.l.o.g.) coprime integers $m,n\in\mathbb{N}$.
its winding number around $(P_1,P_2)=(\frac{b_3}{a_3},\frac{1}{\sqrt{\mu}a_3})$ is $m$.
nodes.label: prop:closed_and_winding_number

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 9
nodes.statement: We first assume that $\gamma$ is closed, i.e. we have $\gamma(s+T)=\gamma(s)$ for all $s\in\mathbb{R}$ and some $T>0$. From Proposition \ref{prop:choice_of_P} we get that $T$ must be a multiple of the period of the curvature function, i.e. $T=2n\sqrt{2-k^2}K(k)$ for some $n\in\mathbb{N}$. Additionally, Theorem \ref{thm:explicit_formula_orbitlike} implies $W_1(s)=W_1(s+T),W_2(s)=W_2(s+T)$ because of $$ \det\matII{a_1}{a_2}{b_1}{b_2} = a_1 b_2-b_1a_2 \stackrel{\eqref{eq:a_1a_2a_3b_1b_2b_3}}{=} \frac{a_1^2+a_2^2}{\sqrt\mu a_3} > 0. $$ Hence, by Proposition~\ref{prop:W1W2_orbitlike}~(v), we have $n\Delta\theta_k\in 2\pi\mathbb{Z}$. Since $\Delta\theta_k$ is positive we find an $m\in\mathbb{N}$ such that $n\Delta\theta_k=2\pi m$, i.e. $k=k_{m,n}$ and $T=\mathcal{L}_{m,n}$ for some $m,n\in\mathbb{N}$ such that $1<\frac{2m}{n}<\sqrt 2$. This proves the necessity of these conditions. Vice versa, $k=k_{m,n}$ is also sufficient for $\gamma_{m,n}$ to be closed. Indeed, from \eqref{eq:def_kappa_orbitlike} and Proposition~\ref{prop:W1W2_orbitlike}~(v) we get that $\kappa,W_1,W_2$ are $\mathcal{L}_{m,n}$-periodic. Hence, $\gamma$ is $\mathcal{L}_{m,n}$-periodic thanks to the explicit formulas from Theorem~\ref{thm:explicit_formula_orbitlike}. \medskip It remains to calculate the winding number of $\gamma:=\gamma_{m,n}$, set $k:=k_{m,n}$. To this end we use the homotopy invariance of the winding number and first calculate the winding number for a more convenient curve, namely (in complex notation) $$ \eta(s):= \gamma_1(s)-\frac{b_3}{a_3} + i\cdot \Big(\gamma_2(s)\frac{\kappa(s)}{\sqrt{\mu}}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{\mu}a_3}\Big). $$ From Theorem~\ref{thm:explicit_formula_orbitlike} we get, using the notation from the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:explicit_formula_orbitlike}, \begin{align*} \eta &= \frac{bW+b_3}{aW+a_3}-\frac{b_3}{a_3} + i \Big( \frac{1}{\sqrt\mu (aW+a_3)} - \frac{1}{\sqrt\mu a_3} \Big) \\ &= \frac{bWa_3 - b_3aW}{a_3(aW+a_3)} - i \frac{aW}{\sqrt\mu a_3(aW+a_3)} \\ &\stackrel{\eqref{eq:a_1a_2a_3b_1b_2b_3}}{=} \frac{a^\perp W}{\sqrt\mu a_3(aW+a_3)} - i \frac{aW}{\sqrt\mu a_3(aW+a_3)} \\ &\stackrel{\eqref{eq:def_theta}}{=} \frac{a_2\sin(\vartheta)+a_1\cos(\vartheta)}{N} + i\cdot \frac{a_1\sin(\vartheta)-a_2\cos(\vartheta)}{N} \end{align*} where $N:= \frac{\sqrt\mu\kappa}{\sqrt{\kappa^2-\mu}} a_3(aW+a_3)$ is a positive and $2n\sqrt{2-k^2}K(k)$-periodic function. Hence, we get from Proposition~\ref{prop:properties_vartheta_orbitlike}~(ii) \begin{align*} \frac{1}{2\pi i} \int_0^{2n\sqrt{2-k^2}K(k)} \frac{\eta'(s)}{\eta(s)}\,ds &= \frac{1}{2\pi i} \int_0^{2n\sqrt{2-k^2}K(k)} \big( - \frac{N'(s)}{N(s)} + i\vartheta'(s)\big) \,ds\\ &= \frac{1}{2\pi} \big(\vartheta(2n\sqrt{2-k^2}K(k))-\vartheta(0)\big) \\ &= \frac{n}{2\pi} \Delta\theta_k, \\ &= m. \end{align*} We now define the homotopy $$ (t,s)\mapsto \gamma_1(s)-\frac{b_3}{a_3} + i\cdot \Big( \gamma_2(s)\big(t\cdot \frac{\kappa(s)}{\sqrt\mu}+1-t\big)-\frac{1}{\sqrt\mu a_3} \Big) $$ that connects the curve $\eta$ (at $t=1$) and the curve $\gamma-P_1-iP_2$ (at $t=0$). We intend to show that this homotopy is admissible, i.e. it is zero-free. To this end we choose $s\in\mathbb{R}$ such that the real part vanishes at $s$ and deduce that the imaginary part is non-zero. For a zero $s\in\mathbb{R}$ of the real part we have $a_3 \gamma_1(s)=b_3$, hence \begin{align*} a^\perp W(s) &\stackrel{\eqref{eq:a_1a_2a_3b_1b_2b_3}}{=} \sqrt\mu a_3 (a_3bW(s) - b_3aW(s)) \\ &= \sqrt\mu (a_3(bW(s)+b_3)-b_3(aW(s)+a_3)) \\ &\stackrel{\eqref{eq:explicit_formula_orbitlike_1}}{=} \sqrt\mu (aW(s)+a_3)(a_3\gamma_1(s)- b_3) \\ &= 0. \end{align*} Due to \eqref{eq:a_1a_2a_3b_1b_2b_3} and Proposition~\ref{prop:W1W2_orbitlike}~(i) this implies $aW(s)= \pm |a||W(s)|= \pm a_3 \sqrt{\kappa(s)^2-\mu}/\kappa(s)$ and thus $$ \gamma_2(s) \stackrel{\eqref{eq:explicit_formula_orbitlike_2}}{=} \frac{1}{\kappa(s)(aW(s)+a_3)} = \frac{1}{a_3(\pm\sqrt{\kappa(s)^2-\mu}+\kappa(s))}. $$ From this we deduce \begin{align*} \gamma_2(s)\big(t\cdot \frac{\kappa(s)}{\sqrt\mu}+1-t\big)-\frac{1}{\sqrt\mu a_3} &= \frac{t(\kappa(s)-\sqrt\mu)+\sqrt\mu -(\pm\sqrt{\kappa(s)^2-\mu}+\kappa(s))}{\sqrt\mu a_3(\pm\sqrt{\kappa(s)^2-\mu}+\kappa(s))} \\ &= \frac{\sqrt{\kappa(s)-\sqrt\mu} \cdot \big( (t-1)\sqrt{\kappa(s)-\sqrt\mu}\mp \sqrt{\kappa(s)+\sqrt{\mu}} \big)}{\sqrt\mu a_3(\pm\sqrt{\kappa(s)^2-\mu}+\kappa(s))} \\ &\neq 0 \end{align*} because of $|(t-1)\sqrt{\kappa(s)-\sqrt\mu}|\leq \sqrt{\kappa(s)-\sqrt\mu}<\sqrt{\kappa(s)+\sqrt\mu}$. Hence, the homotopy is admissible so that the winding number of $\gamma$ around $P$ is $m$.
nodes.statement_short: Periodicity of kappa, W1, W2 gives closedness iff n Delta theta_k in 2 pi Z. The winding number is computed for a homotopic curve eta via vartheta.

nodes.name: number of selfintersections
nodes.statement:
Such a selfintersection occurs if there are $s,t$ with $0\leq s<t<\mathcal{L}_{m,n}$
  and $\gamma_{m,n}(s)=\gamma_{m,n}(t)$. The number of $s$, for which such $t\in (s,\mathcal{L}_{m,n})$ 
  exist, is defined as the number of selfintersections.

nodes.name: Number of selfintersections of gamma_{m,n}
nodes.statement: Let $m,n\in \mathbb{N}$ be coprime such that $1<\frac{2m}{n}<\sqrt 2$. Then the closed orbitlike elastica $\gamma_{m,n}$ has precisely $n(m-1)$ points of selfintersection characterized by the unique solutions $0\leq s<\mathcal{L}_{m,n}$ of the $n(m-1)$ equations \begin{equation} \frac{\vartheta(s)}{\pi} =\frac{(l-1)m}{n}-p \end{equation} where $l,p\in\mathbb{Z}$ satisfy the following conditions: \begin{align} \begin{aligned} l\in\{1,\ldots,2n-1\},\qquad p\in \big\{1,\ldots, \Big\lceil \frac{\min\{l,2n-l\}m}{n}\Big\rceil -1 \big\}. \end{aligned} \end{align}
conclusions: the closed orbitlike elastica $\gamma_{m,n}$ has precisely $n(m-1)$ points of selfintersection
nodes.statement_short: gamma_{m,n} has exactly n(m-1) selfintersections, located at explicit solutions of vartheta(s)/pi = (l-1)m/n - p.

nodes.name: Selfintersection equations
nodes.statement: \frac{\vartheta(s)}{\pi} =\frac{(l-1)m}{n}-p
nodes.label: eq:selfintersections

nodes.name: Conditions on (l,p)
nodes.statement: \begin{aligned} l\in\{1,\ldots,2n-1\},\qquad p\in \big\{1,\ldots, \Big\lceil \frac{\min\{l,2n-l\}m}{n}\Big\rceil -1 \big\}. \end{aligned}
nodes.label: eq:selfintersection_lp_conditions

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 10
nodes.statement: The equality $\gamma(s)=\gamma(t)$ for $0\leq s<t<\mathcal{L}_{m,n}$ is equivalent to $Z(s;P)=Z(t;P)$ for all $P\in\mathbb{R}^2,P_2\neq 0$. Proposition~\ref{prop:formula_Z_orbitlike} and Proposition~\ref{prop:choice_of_P} show that this is in turn equivalent to $\kappa(s)=\kappa(t),W_1(s)=W_1(t),W_2(s)=W_2(t)$. So our aim is to show that these equalities and $0\leq s<t<\mathcal{L}_{m,n}$ are equivalent to \eqref{eq:selfintersections},\eqref{eq:selfintersection_lp_conditions}. The equation $\kappa(s)=\kappa(t)$ and the explicit form of the curvature function from~\eqref{eq:def_kappa_orbitlike} give $$ \text{(i)}\; s= t+2l\sqrt{2-k_{m,n}^2}K(k_{m,n}) \quad\text{or}\quad \text{(ii)}\; s =- t +2l\sqrt{2-k_{m,n}^2}K(k_{m,n}) $$ for some $l\in\mathbb{Z}$. In the case (i) we have by Proposition \ref{prop:W1W2_orbitlike}~(v) $$ W_1(s)+iW_2(s) = (W_1(t)+iW_2(t))e^{il\Delta\theta_{k_{m,n}}} = (W_1(s)+iW_2(s))e^{i\frac{2\pi lm}{n}}. $$ Since $m,n$ are coprime and $s<t$ this implies $l\in -n\mathbb{N}$ and hence $$ s = t + 2l\sqrt{2-k_{m,n}^2}K(k_{m,n}) \leq t - 2n\sqrt{2-k_{m,n}^2}K(k_{m,n}) = t-\mathcal{L}_{m,n} < 0, $$ a contradiction. So this is impossible. In the case (ii) we get from Proposition~\ref{prop:W1W2_orbitlike}~(vi) \begin{align*} i|W(s)|e^{i\vartheta(s)} &\stackrel{\eqref{eq:def_theta}}{=} i(W_2(s)-iW_1(s)) \\ &= W_1(s)+iW_2(s) \\ &\stackrel{\ref{prop:W1W2_orbitlike}.(vi)}{=} \big( -W_1(t) + i W_2(t)\big)e^{i(l-1)\Delta\theta_{k_{m,n}}}\\ &= \big( -W_1(s) + i W_2(s)\big)e^{i\frac{2\pi(l-1)m}{n}}\\ &= i\overline{\big( W_2(s) -i W_1(s)\big)}e^{i\frac{2\pi(l-1)m}{n}}\\ &= i |W(s)| e^{i(-\vartheta(s)+\frac{2\pi(l-1)m}{n})}. \end{align*} This shows that intersection points occur precisely at those $s\in [0,\mathcal{L}_{m,n})$ where \eqref{eq:selfintersections} holds for some $p\in\mathbb{Z}$. Notice that $\vartheta$ is increasing by Proposition~\ref{prop:properties_vartheta_orbitlike} so that a unique solution $s$ in $\mathbb{R}$ exists for any given $p\in\mathbb{Z}$. So it remains to show that the condition~\eqref{eq:selfintersection_lp_conditions} is equivalent to $0\leq s<t<\mathcal{L}_{m,n}$ and that these conditions are satisfied for precisely $n(m-1)$ distinct pairs $(l,p)$. To this end we use Proposition~\ref{prop:properties_vartheta_orbitlike}~(i). Thanks to this result the condition $s\geq 0$ is equivalent to \begin{equation} \vartheta(s) \geq \vartheta(0) = -\frac{\Delta\theta_k}{2}=-\frac{\pi m}{n}. \end{equation} The condition $t<\mathcal{L}_{m,n}$ is equivalent to $s>2(l-n)\sqrt{2-k^2}K(k)$ and thus to \begin{equation} \vartheta(s) > \vartheta(2(l-n)\sqrt{2-k_{m,n}^2}K(k_{m,n})) = \frac{2l-2n-1}{2}\Delta\theta_k = \frac{\pi(2l-2n-1)m}{n}. \end{equation} The last condition $s<t$ holds if and only if $s<l\sqrt{2-k^2}K(k)$ and thus precisely if \begin{equation} \vartheta(s)<\vartheta(l\sqrt{2-k_{m,n}^2}K(k_{m,n}))= \frac{\pi(l-1)m}{n}. \end{equation} Altogether the conditions \eqref{eq:selfintersections1}--\eqref{eq:selfintersections3} and $\vartheta(s) = \frac{\pi(l-1)m}{n} - \pi p$ lead to the conditions $$ 0<p\leq \frac{lm}{n}\quad\text{and}\quad p< \frac{m(2n-l)}{n}. $$ Since $m,n$ are coprime these inequalities for integers $p,l\in\mathbb{Z}$ yield the conditions \eqref{eq:selfintersection_lp_conditions}. Notice that the solutions are different from each other because $m$ and $n$ are coprime. Indeed, if $(l,p),(\tilde l,\tilde p)$ are two pairs satisfying \eqref{eq:selfintersections},\eqref{eq:selfintersection_lp_conditions}, then $l-\tilde l$ is a multiple of $n$, say $l-\tilde l=qn$ for $q\in\mathbb{N}_0$. In the case $q\geq 2$ we get a contradiction due to $$ l = qn+\tilde l \geq 2n+\tilde l > 2n-1. $$ In the case $q=1$ we find $m=p-\tilde p$ and thus a contradiction results from $$ p = \tilde p+m \geq 1+m > \Big\lceil \frac{\min\{l,2n-l\}m}{n}\Big\rceil -1. $$ This proves that we have precisely as many intersection points as pairs $(l,p)$ satisfying \eqref{eq:selfintersection_lp_conditions}. So it remains to show that the number of these pairs is $n(m-1)$. By \eqref{eq:selfintersection_lp_conditions} the number of equations is $$ \sum_{l=1}^{2n-1} \big( \big\lceil \frac{\min\{l,2n-l\}m}{n}\big\rceil -1 \big) = 2\sum_{l=1}^{n-1} \big\lceil \frac{lm}{n}\big\rceil + m -(2n-1) $$ Since $m,n$ are coprime the sum can be computed as follows: \begin{align*} \sum_{l=1}^{n-1} \big\lceil\frac{lm}{n}\big\rceil &= \sum_{l=1}^{n-1} \big\lceil\frac{(n-l)m}{n}\big\rceil \;=\; \sum_{l=1}^{n-1} \big( m + \big\lceil -\frac{lm}{n}\big\rceil \big) \\ &= m(n-1) + \sum_{l=1}^{n-1} \big(-\big\lceil\frac{lm}{n}\big\rceil+1\big) \\ &= (m+1)(n-1) - \sum_{l=1}^{n-1} \big\lceil\frac{lm}{n}\big\rceil. \end{align*} Hence, the number of equations is $m-(2n-1)+(m+1)(n-1)=n(m-1)$, which is all we had to show.
nodes.statement_short: Selfintersection means equal kappa, W1, W2; case analysis on the two kappa-symmetries, then count admissible pairs (l,p).

nodes.name: Condition s >= 0
nodes.statement: \vartheta(s) \geq \vartheta(0) = -\frac{\Delta\theta_k}{2}=-\frac{\pi m}{n}.
nodes.label: eq:selfintersections1

nodes.name: Condition t < L
nodes.statement: \vartheta(s) > \vartheta(2(l-n)\sqrt{2-k_{m,n}^2}K(k_{m,n})) = \frac{2l-2n-1}{2}\Delta\theta_k = \frac{\pi(2l-2n-1)m}{n}.
nodes.label: eq:selfintersections2

nodes.name: Condition s < t
nodes.statement: \vartheta(s)<\vartheta(l\sqrt{2-k_{m,n}^2}K(k_{m,n}))= \frac{\pi(l-1)m}{n}.
